title: The Bookshelf
subtitle: Books that shaped my thinking, challenged my assumptions, or that I simply loved reading.

meta_description: Books Joseph Morante has read, with personal reflections on what each one changed.

books.title: Eleven Rings: The Soul of Success
books.preview: Mastery is not always built by narrowing your focus. Some of the most useful ideas arrive from disciplines that look unrelated to your own.

key_ideas.title: Cross-disciplinary thinking
key_ideas.body: Expertise does not only deepen by narrowing. Music and data science share almost nothing on the surface, but both reward attention to pattern, structure and interpretation. The skill worth developing is recognising the principle two fields have in common and carrying it back into your own work. Being well-rounded is not a detour from mastery; it is what lets you see a solution that a specialist might miss.

key_ideas.title: Audience-centered communication
key_ideas.body: Simplifying an idea is not the same as communicating it. A technically correct explanation still fails if the listener cannot see why it matters to them. Real communication connects the idea to the other person's understanding, priorities and interests.

reflection: One of the most important lessons I took from *Eleven Rings* is that becoming successful in your field, especially as a leader, doesn't necessarily mean focusing exclusively on that field.
Sometimes, the most valuable insights come from disciplines that appear to have absolutely nothing in common with what you do.

Take music and data science, for example. On the surface, music has little to do with AI or advertising technology. But if you look beyond the surface and start thinking more abstractly, you can discover connections in how different disciplines approach patterns, structure, interpretation, and problem-solving.

The important skill isn't simply knowing more about unrelated subjects. It's learning to recognize the underlying principles they share and figuring out how to bring those ideas back into your own work.

That changed how I think about developing expertise. Being well-rounded isn't necessarily a distraction from mastery. Sometimes, it's what allows you to see solutions that someone focused exclusively on one discipline might overlook.
The second lesson that stayed with me was about communication.

I've always valued the ability to explain complicated ideas simply, ideally well enough that a five-year-old could understand them. But I realized that simplicity alone isn't the same as effective communication.
**True communication means connecting an idea to the other person's understanding, priorities, and interests.**
In my work in data science and AdTech, I might be excited about an advanced analytical method that reveals more about the paths consumers take before converting.
From a technical perspective, that can be fascinating. But a client or executive isn't necessarily interested in the sophistication of the underlying model.
They want to understand what the analysis means for their business.
Should they change how they allocate advertising spend? Is a particular campaign underperforming? Are there opportunities to improve results? What should they actually do next?
An explanation can be technically accurate and still fail if the audience doesn't understand why it matters to them.
**My biggest takeaway:** Leadership requires both intellectual breadth and the ability to translate complexity into meaningful action.
It's not just about knowing your subject. It's about recognizing connections others might miss and communicating those connections in a way that helps people make better decisions.

books.title: Born Standing Up: A Comic's Life
books.preview: Patience is the lesson I keep failing to internalise. It took a comedian's account of a decade of methodical practice to make it land.

key_ideas.title: A craft built methodically, not stumbled into
key_ideas.body: Rather than leaning on natural comedic ability, Martin studied, experimented, performed, evaluated what worked and refined. Roughly a decade developing the craft, then several more years refining it before the full rewards arrived. Knowing someone that funny worked that systematically is both insightful and comforting.

key_ideas.title: Hindsight makes a path look inevitable
key_ideas.body: His journey reads as though everything was leading toward the eventual success, and looking back the pieces fit. But living through those years, the outcome was far from obvious; he was figuring it out as he went. It is easy to admire a success when you already know how the story ends, and much harder to trust your own process from somewhere in the middle of it.

reflection: As someone who's dabbled in teaching, DJing, stand-up comedy, and a few other pursuits outside my main career, one lesson I've found particularly difficult to internalize throughout my twenties is patience.
(Haha, saying that makes me sound so old and mature.)

We live in a time when it's almost impossible not to compare ourselves to others. Whether it's LinkedIn, TikTok, or Instagram, there's always someone seemingly further ahead in their career, creative pursuits, or personal life.
And even when you know that everyone has their own journey, it's difficult not to wonder whether you're moving quickly enough or even heading in the right direction.
I've gradually come to recognize that trying to rush the process often does more harm than good. But knowing that intellectually and genuinely believing it are two very different things.

I've watched countless videos about trusting the process, embracing the journey, and being patient with yourself. Yet, somehow, it was Steve Martin's *Born Standing Up* that finally made the lesson resonate.

What fascinated me most was discovering how methodically Martin approached comedy. Rather than relying entirely on natural comedic ability, he studied, experimented, performed, evaluated what worked, and gradually refined his craft.

There was something both insightful and comforting about learning that someone I consider one of the funniest people in the world spent roughly a decade developing his craft, followed by several more years refining it before experiencing the full rewards of that work.
What I particularly loved was how his journey reads almost as though everything was inevitably leading toward his eventual success.
Looking back, the pieces seem to fit together.
But I can only imagine that while he was living through those years, the outcome was far from obvious. He was figuring things out as he went, just like the rest of us.
And that's what stayed with me.
**It's easy to admire someone's success when you already know how their story ends. It's much harder to trust your own process when you're still somewhere in the middle of it.**

Whether I'm developing my technical skills, pursuing research, teaching, or getting behind the decks to DJ, I'm learning that progress doesn't always announce itself. Sometimes, it's simply the accumulation of small improvements, repeated attempts, and lessons that don't seem particularly significant until much later.
Patience isn't about sitting around waiting for something to happen. It's about continuing to practice, experiment, and improve without demanding immediate proof that everything will work out.
And maybe that's something I'll spend the rest of my twenties learning to embrace.
**My biggest takeaway:** Mastery takes time, and the uncertainty of the process doesn't mean you're on the wrong path.

I highly recommend *Born Standing Up*. It's the kind of book I think deserves a place on everyone's bookshelf, whether you're interested in comedy or simply trying to become better at something you care about.

books.title: The Inner Game of Tennis: The Classic Guide to the Mental Side of Peak Performance
books.preview: Stop reading a result as good or bad and read it as information first. Not to suppress the feeling, but to stop the first reaction becoming the final interpretation.

key_ideas.title: Feedback is information before it is a verdict
key_ideas.body: Once every result is labelled good or bad, emotions and judgements attach to the outcome, and those judgements shape how willing you are to experiment or change approach. Something that works today may not work tomorrow, and a disappointing outcome can reveal what a successful one never would. The skill is recognising what you are doing well while staying open to adjustment, whichever way the result felt.

key_ideas.title: A parallel with model training, and its limit
key_ideas.body: A model does not feel disappointed by a wrong prediction or proud of a right one; during training the feedback is simply information used to adjust parameters. Humans are not algorithms and emotions serve purposes far beyond optimising an objective. The borrowable part is narrow: treating results as information before turning them into judgements about yourself.

reflection: One of the most valuable lessons I took from *The Inner Game of Tennis* sounds almost too simple: stop looking at feedback as inherently good or bad. Instead, learn to see it as feedback.
Does that eliminate stress? No.
Does it mean acting like a robot? No.
Does it mean I shouldn't feel disappointed, frustrated, or excited about an outcome? Absolutely not.
At least from my interpretation, that's not what the book is trying to teach.

What resonated with me is the idea that once we label every result as either good or bad, we naturally begin attaching emotions and judgments to those outcomes. And those judgments can influence how willing we are to experiment, change our approach, or recognize what the situation is actually telling us.

If something works, we might become overly attached to the method that produced it. If something doesn't work, we might dismiss the approach entirely, even when there's something valuable to learn from the attempt.
But reality is rarely that straightforward.
Something that works today might not work tomorrow. A disappointing outcome might reveal something important that a successful one never would have.
The challenge is learning to recognize what you're doing well while remaining open to making adjustments, regardless of whether the initial outcome feels positive or negative.
I find an interesting parallel in data science and AI.

A model doesn't need to feel disappointed about an incorrect prediction or proud of a correct one. During training, the feedback provides information that can be used to adjust its parameters or evaluate its performance.
Of course, humans aren't algorithms, and our emotions serve purposes that go far beyond optimizing an objective function.
But I think there's something useful to borrow from that process: **the ability to treat results as information before turning them into judgments about ourselves.**
This is something I'm still actively working on.

As someone developing a career in technology, it's easy to look at an unsuccessful experiment, a project that didn't turn out as expected, or someone else's professional accomplishments and immediately assign meaning to it.
Am I behind? Am I approaching this incorrectly? Should I be further along?
Those questions aren't always helpful, especially when they're driven more by comparison than by what the evidence actually shows.
I'm learning to ask different questions.
What happened? Why might it have happened? What can I learn from it? What should I keep doing, and what should I change?
That doesn't mean suppressing emotions or pretending not to care about outcomes. It means trying not to let my immediate emotional reaction become the final interpretation of an experience.
**My biggest takeaway:** Progress requires being honest about results without allowing those results to define your ability or your worth.
I don't think I've mastered that mindset, and I doubt it's something you simply learn once and never revisit.
But *The Inner Game of Tennis* has helped me approach my career, learning, and personal development with a little more objectivity, curiosity, and willingness to adapt.

books.title: Life for Sale
books.preview: A man puts his life up for sale after a failed suicide attempt, and every absurd thing that follows quietly exposes how much living he still has left in him.

key_ideas.title: An unreliable narrator of his own desires
key_ideas.body: For someone who claims to be ready to give up on life, he keeps landing in situations suggesting something still attaches him to it. He believes what is missing is love. I came away thinking what is missing is excitement, joy and a sense of self-worth, the things that get lost when identity becomes tied to work.

key_ideas.title: The reminder underneath the chaos
key_ideas.body: There is something tragically funny about a character whose attempt to abandon life sends him into experiences that keep showing what life still offers. Don't become so consumed by work that you forget there's a life outside it worth experiencing.

reflection: I've realized that when it comes to fiction, I'm a sucker for the absurd and dark academia. Dark humor, morally complicated characters, and stories that become increasingly ridiculous while somehow revealing something deeply human are right up my alley.
*Life for Sale* might be one of my favorite examples of that.
The premise alone is outrageous: a man decides to put his life up for sale after a failed suicide attempt. What follows is a rollercoaster of increasingly bizarre situations.

But what fascinated me most wasn't necessarily the absurdity of everything happening around him. It was the contradiction between what the protagonist claims to want and what his actions seem to reveal.
In my interpretation, he almost becomes an unreliable narrator of his own desires.

For someone who claims to be ready to give up on life, he continues finding himself in situations that suggest, whether he wants to admit it or not, that there's still something keeping him attached to living.

He seems to believe that what's missing is love. But I came away thinking that perhaps what he's really missing is excitement, joy, and a sense of self-worth that can get lost when so much of your identity becomes tied to work.
That's what made the book resonate with me beyond the entertainment.
There's something almost tragically funny about a character whose attempt to abandon life sends him into experiences that continually expose how much life still has to offer.
And underneath all the chaos, I took away a surprisingly simple reminder:
**Don't become so consumed by work that you forget there's a life outside of it worth experiencing.**
Maybe that's not the only interpretation of the novel, but it's the one that stayed with me.

I would recommend *Life for Sale* to anyone who appreciates absurdist fiction, dark humor, and a story that manages to be entertaining while making you reflect on your own relationship with life and work.

books.title: Lucien
books.preview: Dark academia where the real tension isn't who Lucien turns out to be. It's watching the narrator work to keep believing otherwise.

key_ideas.title: The explanations we reach for
key_ideas.body: Rather than accepting what you are beginning to see about someone, you start finding reasons. Maybe someone else is lying, maybe it's a misunderstanding, maybe the evidence isn't what it looks like. Sometimes we become so invested in our understanding of a person that we spend more energy defending that image than questioning whether it is accurate.

key_ideas.title: The deception you help maintain
key_ideas.body: Most of us have admired or trusted someone, then found parts of their character that did not fit the person we had constructed. Whether we acknowledge that at once or spend time rationalising it is another matter, and the cost of rationalising can land on us.

reflection: *Lucien* was my most recent fiction read at the time of writing this reflection, and I have to say: I loved every second of it.
On the surface, the premise might sound familiar.

A young man enters an affluent world he doesn't fully understand, becomes fascinated by someone who seems to belong there effortlessly, and gradually finds himself caught in a web of manipulation and deception.
It's the kind of setup you'd expect from a dark academia novel.
But what made *Lucien* stand out to me wasn't simply the privileged setting, the deception, or the mystery surrounding its characters.
It was the protagonist's inner thoughts, especially when it came to his friendship with Lucien.
There's something painfully relatable about discovering that someone you consider a friend might not be the person you believed them to be.
And rather than accepting what you're beginning to see, you start finding explanations.
Maybe someone else is lying.
Maybe there's a misunderstanding.
Maybe the evidence isn't what it looks like.
Maybe the person you know couldn't possibly be capable of what others are suggesting.
What fascinated me was watching that internal process unfold.
**Sometimes we become so invested in our understanding of someone that we spend more energy defending that image than questioning whether it's accurate.**
And eventually, we can become the lightning rod for the consequences of another person's actions.

That's what made the story so compelling to me. The psychological tension wasn't just about discovering who Lucien really was. It was about watching the protagonist struggle with what that discovery might mean for his friendship, judgment, and identity.
I think there's something universally human about that experience.
Most of us have encountered someone we admired or trusted, only to discover aspects of their character that didn't fit the person we'd constructed in our minds.
Whether we acknowledge it immediately or spend time rationalizing it is another matter.
For me, *Lucien* captured that experience exceptionally well.
I loved the atmosphere, the character dynamics, and the psychological complexity. It's exactly the kind of dark academia fiction that keeps me reading.
**My biggest takeaway:** Sometimes the hardest deception to recognize is the one we're helping maintain because we don't want our understanding of someone to change.
Highly recommended.

books.title: The New Me
books.preview: Absurdity and dark humour in the strange relationship people have with work, expectations and their own dissatisfaction.
reflection: Both *The New Me* and *Jillian* belong on my bookshelf alongside *Life for Sale*.
I have a soft spot for fiction that finds absurdity and dark humor in everyday life, particularly the strange relationship people have with work, expectations, and their own dissatisfaction.
These are two books I thoroughly enjoyed for that reason.
I'll expand on my individual reflections in the future, but for now, both deserve a place among my fiction favorites.
